title: Boats built without plans
paragraphs: On the south coast of Sulawesi, master builders have made large wooden sailing boats for hundreds of years. The boats are built on the beach, close enough to the water to be pushed into the sea when they are finished. Visitors are often astonished by one fact: for most of that history, the builders have worked without written plans. The shape of the boat is carried in the memory of the head builder, who learned it during many years as an assistant.

The method also differs from what many people expect. In much of the world, boat builders first make a strong frame and then fix the planks to the outside. Here, the order is usually reversed. The shell of planks is built first, and the frame is fitted inside later. The planks are joined with wooden pegs, and the builder judges each curve by eye. Few measurements are written down at any stage.

Building one of these boats can take more than a year. Each stage is marked by ceremonies, which express respect for the wood and for the sea. Although some visitors see these only as colourful traditions, the builders treat them as part of the work. They also bring the whole team together at important moments.

The trade today faces real difficulties. Good timber has become scarce and expensive, and it must often be brought from far away. Some yards now wait months for the right logs to arrive. Many boats that once carried goods have been replaced by steel ships. At the same time, demand has grown from a different direction: tourism companies now order wooden boats for visitors to sail on.

Not everyone is sure that this is a good thing. Tourist boats need engines, cabins and other features that the old designs did not include. Some builders enjoy the challenge, while others worry that the old knowledge will slowly be lost. For now, the yards remain busy, and young assistants continue to learn beside the masters.
